headline: Referred proposed ban on data centers for review; public hearing held on removing two-family parking minimums.
summary: The first proposal would define data centers and prohibit them in every Salem zoning district. The second would remove parking minimums for two-family homes, according to Councilor King. The minutes record a referral vote for the data center proposal but no recorded vote on the parking motion.
decisions: Referred the proposed data center zoning ordinance for review, all in favor.

decision_evidence.quote: Councilor Varella motions to refer the matter to the Planning Board, all in favor

CITY OF SALEM  
SEPTEMBER 9, 2026 
JOINT PUBLIC HEARING OF THE  
CITY COUNCIL AND THE PLANNING BOARD 
 
A Joint Public Hearing of the Salem City Council and the Planning Board was held in person  on 
Wednesday, September 9, 2026, at 6:00 P .M. in accordance with Chapter 40A, Section 5, of the 
Massachusetts General Laws for the purpose of discussing two (2) diﬀerent proposed Zoning 
Ordinance Amendments relative to Data Centers and Parking Spaces, Parking and Loading and 
Development Standards.  
 
Absent were Councilor Prosniewski 
 
Council President  Alice Merkl presiding 
 
The following Planning Board Members were present: Chair Kirt Rieder, Vice Chair Sarah Tarbet, 
Jonathan Berk, Elena Eimert, Tom Furey, and Helen Sides 
 
Absent were Josh Turiel 
Arriving late were Zach Caunter at 6:16 p.m. 
 
Also, in attendance were Mayor Dominic Pangallo, and Amy Kwesell of KP Law

SUMMARY 
 
1st Zoning Ordinance  
 
Section I. Section 3.1 Table of Principal and Accessory Use Regulations of the City of Salem Zoning 
Ordinance is hereby amended by adding in Section D industrial Uses, after “Contractor’s Yard; 
landscaping business,” the following, shown in underline and italics: 
 
  
 
Section II. Section 10.0 Definitions is hereby amended by inserting the following definition 
after the definition for “COOP”: 
 
Data Center: A facility, or portion thereof, primarily designed or used to house computer 
servers and related information technology infrastructure for the storage, processing, 
management, or transmission of electronic data. A Data Center may include, but is not 
limited to, server racks, data storage systems, cooling systems, power conditioning 
equipment, substations, uninterruptible power supplies, backup generators, 
telecommunications equipment, security systems, and associated mechanical and electrical 
infrastructure. For purposes of this ordinance, a Data Center shall not be considered an 
Office, Warehouse, Manufacturing, or Research use. Notwithstanding anything herein to 
the contrary, Data Centers are prohibited in each and every underlying district, overlay 
district and special district of this Ordinance. 
 
Section III. This Ordinance shall take effect as provided by City Charter 
 
Mayor Pangallo states that the city has received positive feedback on this ordinance and makes 
clear that the language does not prevent the creation of server rooms for businesses. He states 
that the town of Mansfield established a threshold of two (2) megawatts of demand at full build 
out; Shutesbury established a definition based on square footage. Both of these bylaws were 
approved by the Attorney General’s office. As the city’s code does not speak to data centers, it is 
not an allowable use, this ordinance is created out of an abundance of caution and is seeking to 
define AI data centers and prohibit them. The impacts of the centers have become clear and are 
not impacts that should be invited into Salem. He does not believe that the city is starved for 
economic activity. Nor does he believe there is a way to set guardrails for the largest of these

facilities that will not be challenged or litigated by those who stand to gain the most. The 
industrial history of the city left the ground poisoned and inhibited the ability to build homes and 
renovate parks and the shoreline.   
 
Councilor King is curious how the Mayor feels about the executive order requiring that requires 
datacenters to have local approval before state permitting. Mayor Pangallo defers to Attorney 
Kwesel. The executive order does not have any impact on this ordinance. The order is for larger 
centers and that definition is much narrower.  
 
Councilor Sydoriak asks how this would impact the opportunity to have a hospital, etc.? Mayor 
Pangallo says that the direction that Mansfield and Shutesbury went (size or energy usage) could 
be part of the Planning Board’s recommendation back to Council. Attorney Kwesel says any use 
that is currently permitted would be a legacy use. And anyone applying for a permit prior to July 
1, has this legacy status. She qualifies that something like a hospital would be excluded as data 
storage is not the primary use. Councilor Sydoriak asks where data centers could be placed if the 
ordinance does not pass. Attorney Kwesel says that right now they are prohibited everywhere in 
Salem, however many municipalities are creating ordinances out of an abundance of caution, to 
avoid future building commissioners from interpreting the zoning differently. 
 
Councilor Smith asks if  “portion thereof primarily designed for,” means a room or a separate 
structure; Attorney Kwesel says they anticipate a separate structure. Mr. Smith asks if there are 
any active permits right now. He is concerned that people may scramble to get their data centers 
open before the ordinance passes. Ms. Kwesel says that the executive order would also hold up 
the data centers as it does require a community benefits agreement (CBA).  
 
Councilor Holappa asked the Mayor if he has spoken with the building commissioner; he has and 
his interpretation of the conversation is that this is codifying for the future.  
 
Councilor King says there are basically five (5) buckets data centers fall into: enterprise, co-
location, edge, modular, and hyperscale. Suggests regulating data centers based on the types and 
allowing smaller scale here to avoid more pressure to have larger scale elsewhere. Mayor Pangallo says 
there was discussion on the categories but tying it to the physical characteristics of the building 
(square footage or power draw) is more consistent in the future.  
 
Councilor King thinks that the benefits for the energy grid/environment are valid but would 
encourage any variant of the language to include an offset. Pushes back on the concept on the 
idea of Salem not having any data centers and expresses concern that banning them in one spot 
puts a burden on another. Believe that reasonable and high expectation language could be 
drafted.  
 
Councilor Sydoriak asks why more flexibility wasn’t considered via the special permit process. 
Mayor Pangallo says that the special permit process creates another burden for the business

owner. He doesn’t think there is a reasonable offset to allow this, that CBAs will be challenged in 
court, and the legislature can reverse what was passed. 
 
PLANNING BOARD COMMENTS 
 
Ms. Tarbet wonders if  environmental impact is the thing that is most concerning. Is there a 
mechanism to prevent that rather than the label of data center.  Mayor Pangallo says that there 
are exiting regulations to environmental impacts. This is an industry that demonstratively affects 
communities and water and electricity. And after construction generates very little employment.  
 
Mr. Rieder tripped up by the facility or portion thereof making it seem to be about new 
construction of a certain size. Would like the prohibition to cover data centers added to existing 
buildings and would like regulation based on square footage. Water usage is the biggest concern 
as new technologies could increase energy efficiency surrounding electricity. Of particular 
concern is the adaptive reuse of buildings like the old telephone switching center. Highly unlikely 
that salt water can be used. Attorney Kwesel says the ordinance would apply to adaptive reuse as 
it would be a new use and must be a use that is allowed. On mitigation, there is no way that some 
of the facilities can be mitigated. Anticipates CBAs to be “let us do what we want, and we will pay 
you something.”  
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
 
Steve Kapantais 
Wisteria Street  
 
Thinks the wrong questions are being asked. He hears comments that salt water can’t be used, 
when a data center in Portugal has been constructed to use salt water. The technology 
surrounding data centers is changing rapidly and believes a 365-day moratorium would be a 
better path – allowing the city to become better educated. Construction jobs are needed in the 
city, and data centers would provide them. Finds discussion on water usage to be incongruous as 
37% of the water delivered to Salem is lost, up nearly 120% from six (6) years ago.  
 
George Burden 
 
Finds interesting that they are looking at banning something using a lot of land and not creating a 
lot of jobs and not sure we need to ban data centers might be something that people in Salem 
might prefer as they don’t increase traffic. 
 
Councilor Varella motions to close the public hearing,  all in favor 
 
Councilor Varella motions to refer the matter to the Planning Board, all in favor   
 
 Jonathan Berk motions to close the public hearing, seconded by Graham Wing, all in favor

Section I. Amend Section 5.1.8 Table of Required Parking Spaces by

Section II. Amend Section 6.11.8 Parking and Loading 
a. Inserting the phrase "and two-family dwelling units" after “For multifamily dwelling 
units” at the beginning of the section. 
 
Section III. Amend Section 8.7.8.4 Development Standards. Parking Standards Section 
B. Parking Ratios, section i 
a. by inserting the phrase "and two-family dwellings" after “For multifamily 
dwellings” 
Section IV. This Ordinance shall take effect as provided by City Charter. 
 
Councilor King says the language at the heart of the ordinance  removes parking minimums for 
two (2) family homes. Council reviewed parking minimums for residential multifamily housing, 
with the key being that those changes were only for multifamily housing (3+ units). The goal is to 
close a loophole. Today, single family homes require two (2) spots and for a two (2) family, three 
(3) spots are required.  The removal of parking minimums was partially to spur development as 
parking costs money. She reminds that this  doesn’t ban parking  but rather gives ﬂexibility to 
builders based on where the project is located . A conversation about parking is also a 
conversation of housing. The Planning Department not able to attend  tonight and directed 
Council to the resources at Imagine Salem and the Housing Roadmap. The research already exists 
to support this ordinance.  
 
Councilor Sydoriak believes that two (2) family dwellings were left out of the previous ordinance 
intentionally. Would like to exercise caution regarding the word “loophole.” This is piggybacking 
on a thorough study.  
 
Councilor Holappa asks a series of hypothetical questions and provides a brief history of why we 
have parking minimums. But ultimately asks if these parking minimums are serving the

Last year’s study showed that there were two  (2) factors most considered: how aﬄuent the

Councilor Turowski is grateful that Councilor King brought this forward. Says that c onstituents

Councilor Smith says that by looking at the chart, three plus ( 3+), multifamily dwellings are 
incentives for development so if you are thinking of two (2) or three (3) family  home, you will go 
with a three (3) family. This could have been something they through about. The other concern 
is the free market around parking is not actually free; there are developers who seek to  maximize

Councilor Merkl cautions against the expectation of the Planning Departments attendance at the 
meeting. They were not brought in to speak, and this is merely the beginning of the process. 
There will be other times.  
 
Councilor Holappa questions “what’s the worst it can happen?” And asks how many new units

Councilor King echoes that the Planning Department has been helpful answering questions  and

Councilor Flynn is concerned that people will still have cars and move here with cars and will park 
in other neighborhoods ; plus, their own visitors . Its not fair to say that it won’t be an 
inconvenience for others. There is reason why they did this with two (2)-family houses and would 
like to know the reasons why they did that. Deﬁnitely not a loophole.  
 
PLANNING BOARD COMMENTS 
 
Mr. Berk says that a lot of the data a year ago was from other cities  but now Salem has a year’s 
worth of data. We see buildings near the train with less parking, building s far from train  with 
more parking. Small developers charge more for housing with parking. There are concerns that 
should be addressed but there is data to support the removal of all parking.  
 
Ms. Eimert, not speaking as a former member of the Planning Department but as someone who 
was involved in the previous ordinance. Says that the work was g uided by the greatest possible 
impact, multifamily housing, and to reduce risk of overparking. The previous project partnered

with the Massachusetts Area Planning Council (MAPC) Perfect Fit Study and built on their dataset. 
Findings support for reduction in parking in duplexes. Many households have one (1) or fewer 
cars. Building excess parking attracts cars. Think about ﬂexible designs to build housing in areas 
that make sense for car free . D uplex and two ( 2) family homes provide aﬀordable home 
ownership. This is what people want.  A lot of parking challenges we have are an issue of 
allocation, not supply. Encouraging parking in wrong locations doesn’t meet needs. Also, a city 
wide resident parking permit system would be better than the patchwork system.  
 
Mr. Wing says that this doesn’t  incentivize anything as multifamily housing is not allowed in R2 
zones. A lot of housing doesn’t meet this at all; there are plenty of houses on his street that have 
one (1) or three (3) cars.  
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
 
Polly Wilbert 
7 Cedar Street 
 
Missing information. Would like the Planning Department to share with Council  on a quarterly 
basis a spreadsheet on the status of the Housing Roadmap. There is already not enough snow 
emergency parking. People who work in Salem park in neighborhoods further constraining the 
neighborhoods. Experiences her driveway being blocked often. There is a demographic issue - a 
fair number of seniors rely on their cars to get them to opponents and avoid isolation. If they live 
in a dense part of city , they need their cars close by . How many new jobs have been created in 
Salem that can support a family successfully? Many people will need to commute elsewhere. Not 
all jobs are on public transport. People who need to make a living make the traﬃc in and out of 
the city. Constraining parking constrains economic success. Get more information on the impact 
on this.  
 
Councilor King moved to close the public hearing,  all in favor
